newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: U.N. witness says Bosnian guard scarred him for life.
newsitem.headline: U.N. witness says Bosnian guard scarred him for life.

text.p: An elderly Serb witness told the U.N. criminal tribunal for former Yugoslavia on Tuesday that a Bosnian Moslem camp guard in the dock on warcrimes charges beat him so badly in 1992 that he was scarred for life.

Writing notes in the dock, shaven-headed Esad "Zenga" Landzo looked on while Bosnian Serb Branko Gotovac testified about his treatment at the Moslem/Croat run Celebici prison camp in central Bosnia during the summer of 1992.

Landzo faces warcrimes charges with fellow Moslems, deputy Celebici camp commander Hazim Delic and regional Moslem military commander Zejnil Delalic. Also in the dock is Zdravko Mucic, the Croat commander of the prison camp which had previously been a Yugoslav Army fuel depot.
Gotovac, now 66, clearly identified Landzo and related how he had threatened to kill him.
"I know him very well because he caused me a great deal of harm. He injured me and my human dignity. He said I would be dead within eight days," said Gotovac.

Landzo, who was aged 19 at the time he is accused of murdering and torturing Serbs at the camp, beat the elderly man so hard that he swallowed his own tongue and could only be revived after a fellow prisoner, a male nurse, prised the tongue out with a shoe horn.
"I had to put my hands behind my head then he kicked me in the testicles. During all this my tongue went back inside my throat. I was urinating blood," Gotovac said.

Responding to cross examination from Landzo's defence lawyer, Cynthia White McMurrey of the U.S., Gotovac said Landzo burned him with a lighted cigarette so badly that he still cannot move all the fingers properly on one hand.
Other lasting injuries were a shoulder that still gave him pain and a rip in the wall of his stomach that left his intestines pressing against the skin without full support.
"Before this I was as healthy as steel," he said.
Teresa McHenry, one of the prosecution lawyers, challenged McMurrey for repetitive questioning which amounted to witness harrassment.
Minutes later presiding judge Adolphus Karibi-Whyte of Nigeria issued a stinging rebuke to McMurrey for her approach.
"I have left you at large when some of the things you have said have been complete rubbish. If you continue being irresponsible I think I will have to take a different attitude," said Karibi-Whyte.
The Celebici proceedings are the first group trial by the tribunal which was established by the United Nations Security Council in May 1993.

As of March 3, 1996 the tribunal had indicted 75 suspects -- 54 Serbs (one of whom has since died), 18 Croats and three Moslems. One man has been convicted and sentenced to 10 years in jail, a verdict is expected soon in another case.
The two most prominent indicted suspects are former Bosnian Serb leader Radovan Karadzic and former Bosnian Serb military commander Ratko Mladic, both of whom remain at large.
